translations.text: A discourse of our holy father Basil on the beginning of the Proverbs of Solomon.
The fruit of obedience is good. So let us be obedient to our sweet father, who has set before us a task drawn from the words of the Spirit,
and who, like a hunter experienced in difficult terrain, is as it were making trial of the running of a royal [?], in order to learn the swiftness of its running.
He has set before us the interpretation of the beginning of the "Proverbs," and how hard it is to find the force of this saying is known to everyone who has examined it even a little.
Yet let us not be negligent in undertaking this task, with hope in the Lord, who through the prayer of that shepherd will give us speech at the opening of our mouth.
We see three books of the all-wise Solomon: first this one, the "Proverbs"; second, that of "Ecclesiastes"; and third, the "Song of Songs."
And each has its own form and character of subject matter.

For the book of Proverbs is a teaching of right order and of battle against the passions, and an instruction for life, which speaks of the things that ought to be done and those that ought to be fled from;
"Ecclesiastes" engages in natural philosophy and reveals to us the vanity of the affairs of this world,
so that we may not regard this transitory world as something good, nor spend the care of the soul on these vain things;
and the "Song of Songs" shows the pattern of the perfection of souls, for in it is the speech and the character of the union of bride and bridegroom.
That is, the union of the soul with the Word of God, the Lord of all. But let us turn to the matter before us.
"The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David, who became king over Israel."
A "proverb" is a profitable saying whose force is hidden: it is useful and good even when understood plainly as it stands, but its great force lies in its depth.
For this reason the Lord also said: "All this I have said in proverbs. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak in proverbs, but will speak to you openly,"
and he said this because in the saying of a proverb there is no openness; rather, it reveals its force in a hidden way to those who search it out.
And he says "Proverbs of Solomon," that is, words of teaching, good and useful in all of human life,
and he added his own name as well, so that the reader may hear his name first and know whose saying it is.
And in this way he will listen to the words with trust and gladly, for the trustworthiness of the teacher makes the word more acceptable and makes the hearers listen well.
So they are the "Proverbs of Solomon," of that Solomon to whom the Lord said: "Behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart;
there has been no other like you before you, and after you no other like you shall arise." And again it is written:
"The Lord gave Solomon wisdom and very great understanding, and breadth of heart like the sand on the seashore.
And the wisdom of Solomon increased beyond the wisdom of all the men of former times, and beyond all the wise men of Egypt."
Thus it is good to state his name at the very beginning of the discourse, so that you may understand who the speaker is: "The Proverbs of Solomon, son of David."
The name of his father is also written, so that you may know that Solomon was wise, born of a wise and prophetic father, from whom he had learned the holy Scriptures from childhood.

And he did not receive the kingship by seizure, nor did he, being a stranger to it, take the honor of kingship by tyranny; rather, by the just judgment of his father and the command of God he took up that ancestral honor.
This man became king over Israel. Nor is this statement idle; it is there so that he may be clearly distinguished from others,
should anyone else be called by his name, and also because of the building of that glorious temple, so that you may know who made it and who was the cause of all the good order of that city.
And this too is a great help toward accepting his words: that they were spoken by a king.
For if kingship is lawful authority, it is evident that by a king who is truly worthy of this name,
the teachings spoken by him are good and lawful, speak what is better for all, and are written down not for his own profit but for the good of all others.
For by this the tyrant is distinguished from the king: the tyrant is he who in every way seeks only his own interest and has no concern for others, whether they are harmed or not;
but a king is he who seeks what is better for those under him.
So now he first states the good things contained in this book, how many good things are given to those who listen to it.
And first, through these proverbs wisdom and instruction are known. Now wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human matters and of their causes.
For whoever speaks rightly about God knows wisdom, as blessed Paul says:
"We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are passing away,
but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, hidden, which God ordained beforehand, before the ages."
And again, whoever understands the Creator from the creation of the world has also come to know God through the wisdom of the world,
"for his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are seen, being known through the things that are made."
And again, he leads us to understanding of God through his words, in which he says:
"God by wisdom founded the earth," and again:
"When he was preparing the heaven, I was with him," and: "I was with him, fitting things together, and I was the one in whom he rejoiced."
For he said all this as if from the mouth of Wisdom, in order to declare its meaning well, and above all where he says:
"The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways." He says this about the wisdom that appears in the world, as if it were crying out through these visible things
that it was created by God, and that this great wisdom in created things does not exist of itself.
For just as "the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament the work of his hands," and they speak without voice,
since "there are no speeches nor words whose voice is not heard," so too are the words of that firstborn Wisdom.
That which was sown in the world at creation before the others preaches in silence its Maker and Lord, so that through it you may ascend to the understanding of the only Wise One.
But there is also a human wisdom: experience in the affairs of this world, on account of which we call those who are knowledgeable in the arts of the world wise.
For this reason also the invitation to wisdom is spoken of in lofty terms in this book, for:
"Wisdom is praised in the ways out, and in the streets she takes boldness, and on the tops of the walls she is proclaimed."
For he saw the nature of human beings, that we all love it and that wisdom is glorious among people.
Therefore, by that praise of wisdom he also teaches souls not to strive for its acquisition lazily and carelessly.
And he says that she is great in every place: on the roads and in the streets and in the strongholds of the city. For this reason he names gates and streets and walls.
And by the ways out and the streets he signifies her glory, and by the walls her benefit and her help toward all firmness.
And he wants us to hold her dear; for this reason he says:
"Say to wisdom that she is your sister," and again he says: "Love her, and she will guard you."
And then he shows her benefit to all, and that she bestows her good on everyone equally. For this reason he said:
"She has slaughtered her young animals," that is, she has prepared good and solid food for those whose power of soul and whose senses have been trained; and that:
"She has poured her wine into the cup, which gladdens the heart of man." And by the cup he means the common and shared reception of good things,
from which it is possible for all to receive equally, according to the capacity of each; and that:
"She has prepared her table." He says all of this in parable and through bodily things shows us what is spiritual, for he names the rational food of the soul a table,
to which she calls with a lofty proclamation, that is, with perfect teaching of good deeds, in which there is nothing low or worthless.
"You who are foolish, turn to me." For as the sick need a physician, so the foolish need wisdom; and again, that:
"Buying her is better than treasures of gold and silver," and:
"She is more precious than precious stones," and: "Nothing precious is worthy of her," and:
"Son, if you become wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors also," and that, "The deeds of a wise child will prosper."
And so it is possible for you to investigate at leisure what is said in it by Solomon about wisdom, and to understand the truth of the saying.
"Since, then, wisdom will not enter a soul that does evil," for this reason he first purifies through the fear of God the souls of those into whom wisdom is going to enter.
For sowing the mysteries of life in this way among the unpurified and unprepared, and admitting everyone alike, those who neither by deed
…nor have they been purified by the word, he is like a man who pours very costly ointment into unclean vessels. Therefore he says:
"The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord," and the fear of the Lord purifies souls, as in the prayer of the prophet, who says:
"Nail my flesh to your fear," for where that fear dwells, there is all purity of soul,
since everything impure and every evil deed has been put to flight, and the members of the flesh, being nailed to the fear of God, cannot be stirred toward evil deeds.
For just as someone who has been nailed with a physical nail is idle for every kind of work, gripped by pains,
so too whoever has been nailed to the fear of the Lord is unable to look with his eye toward any improper thing,
or to stretch out his hands toward evil, or to do anything else that is not good that a person may do,
when he is gripped by the expectation of those torments that have been spoken of, as if by pains and bitter aches.
But the defiled and wicked it drives out from that good school, and it says:
"Let the fearless keep to the gates," and: "You will seek wisdom among the wicked and will not find it," and again:
"The wicked will seek me and will not find me," for they have not been purified by the fear of God.
Now therefore, whoever intends to come to that teaching of wisdom, let him purify the filth of sin by that divine fear, and in this way let him approach.
And thus this other good has become evident to us: the attainment of the fear of God through the teaching of the parables, which has come from wisdom.
Again, the second of its promises was the understanding of discipline.
Now discipline is a training for the benefit of the soul, which purifies it by toil and affliction from the stains of sin,
"which at the time does not appear to be a cause of joy, but afterward gives the fruit of peace to those who have been tested by it, for their life."
And the understanding of such discipline is not the work of a simple mind,
for many, in toil and in affliction lasting a short time, become faint-hearted and, out of foolishness, do not wait for the benefit that comes at the end,
but flee from the affliction of discipline, and so remain in the disease of being undisciplined.
Therefore the words of the saints are to be marveled at, how they say:
"Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath," for it is not discipline that they flee, but wrath.
And similar to this is the saying that declares:
"Discipline us, Lord, but with justice and not with wrath and anger," and again: "The discipline of the Lord opens my ears."
For just as little children, when they grow faint-hearted about learning, after the beating that their teachers or tutors inflict on them,
become careful and begin to learn diligently, and the word that was disregarded before the beating,
after the beating, as though their ears had only then been opened, is in this way accepted and kept in memory,
The same thing happens to those who are disobedient to divine instruction, who despise his commandments: when reproof comes upon them from God,
then, even by force, those commandments of God which are constantly spoken and preached come to be accepted, as though their ears had been opened only then.
For this reason he says: "The instruction of the Lord opens my ears."
For instruction corrects the disorderly, as Paul did when he handed the disorderly over to the devil, as to some cruel tormentor,
so that in this way they might learn not to blaspheme; and it turns back the one who has fallen away, as it is said: "After his captivity he repented."
And it is good to know the term "instruction" and for how many things it is good. Solomon knew its benefit and says:
"Do not cease to discipline a child, for if you strike him with a rod, he will not die;
for you strike him with the rod, but you have saved his soul from death," and "for what son is there whom his father does not discipline?"
For those who understand well, this instruction is more precious than great wealth. Therefore Solomon says:
"Receive instruction and not silver," so that in a time of affliction, when either the body is weak or something else happens, you may not take up an evil thought against God,
but may accept with great patience those blows that have come upon you for your sins, and may you too say, with that understanding that comes from instruction:
"I have borne the wrath of the Lord, because I sinned against him," and: "It is good for me that you have humbled me," as was the blessed Paul, who said:
"Disciplined and not killed," and: "When we are reproved by the Lord, we are being disciplined."
Further, the receiving of learning is also called instruction, as it is said of Moses: "He was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians."
For it is not entering into vain studies, but the understanding of good teachings, that is no small path of life.
For see, some have occupied themselves with the art of measuring the earth, which the Egyptians discovered, or with the reckoning of the stars,
which the Chaldeans honor, and so through those vain things they have been drawn away from the study of the divine words.
And rhetoric, declamation and philosophy have also kept many from having leisure, and the substance of these is falsehood,
for declamation does not exist without fables, nor philosophy without the deceitful twisting of words.
Since, then, through their zeal for these many things they became negligent of understanding divine teaching, for they grew old in the pursuit of those vain things,
therefore the understanding that comes from instruction is good for choosing what is good and for fleeing from what is useless and harmful.
and again, knowledge of the words of wisdom comes through the proverbs to anyone who listens to them well, for there is an understanding of what is better, as it is said:
"Be children in wickedness, but mature in mind."
Wisdom, then, is one of those primary virtues that are the parents of the other virtues, by which we come to know good and evil.
But how is it that it is said of the serpent that it was wiser than all the beasts, and again the Lord says:
"Be wise as serpents," and again that unjust steward is called wise?
But it is evident that wisdom is of two kinds: for one kind is the seeking of one's own advantage at the harm of one's neighbor, such as that of the serpent,
which protects itself, and again, that resourcefulness in affairs which gains one's own advantage, such as the conduct of that steward.
But the second is true wisdom, which is the knowledge of the things that ought to be done and those that ought not.
And whoever follows such wisdom will never depart from works of virtue, nor ever draw near to the evil of sin.
And whoever understands the words of wisdom knows which words are contrived and deceitful,
or which are true, and like a skilled merchant he distinguishes the bad from the good: he throws away the bad and acquires the good.
This wisdom grants to the one who acquires it to lay his foundation upon the rock, which is faith in Christ, so that he may be unshaken in the times of rain and wind.
For unshakenness under trials is thus depicted by the Lord in this parable, and it teaches us not to be negligent in good works,
but to be prepared beforehand in expectation of the coming of the bridegroom, as it is said:
Those wise virgins went in with the bridegroom, since they had oil in their vessels,
but the foolish ones, because of their unpreparedness, were cast outside the bridal chamber and became strangers to that joy.
After this let us see what is meant by the acceptance of the turnings of words.
For the true word, which proceeds from a good mind, is simple and clear and always stands firm upon one thing,
but the perverse word, spoken with artifice, has much elaborate composition, changes into many forms, and has countless turnings, for it changes its color to please its hearers.
But proverbs are of great profit to us, so that through them we may be able to withstand those who speak to us with the artifice of the world.
For whoever listens to these and is armed with their teaching is able to endure the turnings of words unharmed, so that he is not swayed by them from the truth.
For when deeds are of one form and words say something else, that is a turning, or rather an overturning, of the truth.
And again, whoever appears in one form and in truth has another form uses the turnings of words to deceive those who see him,
as hares and foxes do to the dog, showing it one path and turning aside another way.
And again, the turning of words is the opposition that those false wise men raise against the truth, who do not accept the simplicity of spiritual teaching,
who are sharpened for opposition by inventiveness of speech and often conceal the power of the truth with much talk.
But one who is strengthened by the proverbs stands against such turnings and, even if the words on both sides appear equal, he will be able to find the one.
And again, these Proverbs also grant the understanding of true justice.
For justice is a thing that disposes matters according to worth, and this thing is difficult:
first, because, owing to a deficiency of wisdom, it is hard to find how to give to each one fairly according to his worth; and again,
because through the passions justice is hidden from people, and they disregard the poor, while they do not rebuke the rich who do evil.
But the book of Proverbs says that it gives the knowledge of that true justice to all who obey it.
And since many are lovers of display, and in deed commit injustice while in word they praise justice,
let the one taught by the Proverbs not be ignorant of these people either, but let him know which is the deceitful kind and which is true justice.
And since many of the wise men of this world have said concerning justice that no one is able to find that true justice,
this wise man shows us the finding of that true justice. Now one justice is this one that exists among us: giving equitably.
For even though we cannot find the true form of it, yet when we act with a God-fearing mind, our deed does not become useless.
And again, another justice is that which comes from heaven from the just Judge, the justice that sets right and repays,
whose working is hidden and hard to see because of its height; and for this reason the Psalmist said: "Your righteous judgments are like the mountains of God."
But this book promises us the revealing of that true justice, for those who understand well the teaching of these Proverbs.
For since some sins are committed involuntarily and some through the wickedness of one's own will, so too their judgments are not the same.
For let us speak of the judgment that is to come for fornication, and of two prostitutes:

one of them had been sold into prostitution and is in sin by compulsion, and under compulsion she gives over the use of her body to that evil master; while the other, for the sake of filthy pleasure, is in that sin willingly.
How then could their judgment be one and the same? Again, one person sinned who was brought up from childhood in evil custom, and who came from evil parents
into this world and was raised among words and deeds of defilement; while another had many things drawing him toward virtue:
a good upbringing, the excellence of his teachers, the hearing of good and divine words, orderliness in food,
the teachings of his parents, and the other things by which virtue of soul comes about; and yet he too fell into the same sin.
How would this man not justly deserve heavier torments? For the one would be punished only for the means of life
that are sown in our nature, because he did not use them well; whereas this second man would be judged for what we have said,
and besides this, also because he made vain the help that was given him for his life, and by his wickedness went over to sin.
Now then, the knowledge of that true justice is difficult, and it requires a great, lofty and perfect mind.
And again, a promise of attaining theology is also found in these "Proverbs", for that true righteousness is Christ,
"who became for us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption."
Again, the right direction of judgment is also joined to the knowledge of that true righteousness, for it is impossible
that one who has not first been taught in righteousness should judge disputed matters well.
For even Solomon, if he had not had those words of justice within himself,
would not have been able to render so well that famous judgment which he gave to the harlots concerning the child.
For since neither had witnesses and the truth of neither was evident, he then turned to nature, and through it he found out what was unknown:
for the stranger accepted the killing of the child unmoved and without pain,
but the true mother could not bear even to hear of the matter, because of her natural love and mercy.
Now then, whoever knows true righteousness is also able to direct judgment rightly.
For just as an archer aims his arrow at what he intends to shoot, and avoids its passing above
or below, or to that side or this, but looks straight, so the judge of righteousness acts.
He acts neither with partiality, for partiality in judgment is evil, nor again with rancor, but when he judges between the two,
the oppressor and the oppressed, he takes away from the one who has excess as much as the lesser lacks, and makes them equal.
But whoever does not have that true righteousness in his soul, but looks either to a bribe, or to friendship,
or to enmity, does not judge rightly. Of such a person the Psalmist said:
"If you truly practised righteousness, you would judge uprightly, O sons of men."
For rightness of judgment reveals rightness of mind, as this all-wise one himself says further on:
"A large and a small balance are abominable to the Lord," and by "balance" he speaks figuratively of injustice in judgment.
And this is needed not only by judges but by everyone in distinguishing matters, for each person has in his own nature a tribunal by which good is distinguished from evil.
And it is good for us to judge justly and fittingly in matters and, like good judges, to honor virtue and punish wickedness.
For example, let us say that chastity and fornication are being judged by you, and your mind sits on high and that tribunal has been entrusted to it,
and desire assists sin, while the fear of God stands with chastity.
Then, if you condemn sin and give the victory to chastity, you have rendered a righteous judgment;
but if you give the victory to desire and honor sin, you have perverted that judgment and have become liable to the curse of the one who says:
"Woe to those who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter, who call light darkness and darkness light."
Since then, as Solomon himself says, "The thoughts of the righteous are just," for this reason diligence is required,
so that in the court of the soul the judgments of deeds may be made with justice, and so that the mind may be like a pair of scales, weighing each deed justly.
And when each commandment within you disputes with the sin opposed to it, give the law of God the victory over sin.
If greed and justice are contending within you, pass a sentence of punishment on the desire for other people's possessions and give honor to virtue.
Again, if patience and impatience are disputing within you, put impatience to shame and honor patience.
Likewise, if enmity and love are doing this, treat the one with contempt and banish it to a distant land, but embrace love as your own.
Or if faithlessness and sincerity, wisdom and folly, justice and injustice, purity and fornication, and every virtue stand against every evil within you,
then show the justice of your judging in the inner court of the soul, keep the commandment of justice with you, and show your hatred of evil,
when you turn sin away and honor virtue.
For if in every matter you give virtue the victory within you, you will be blessed "on that day of judgment,
when God judges the hidden things of people according to this gospel of ours, and among one another your thoughts accuse you or justify you."
And then you will not depart in shame for having inclined toward sin, but you will be honored with the crown of righteousness, with which you crowned the righteousness of the days of your life.
And then you will know what good things this book of Proverbs has procured for you, which taught you true justice and the right direction of judgment.
Again, what is there beyond all this? Hear how he says:
"To give shrewdness to the innocent, and knowledge and understanding to the young child."
But we understand innocence in two ways: either it speaks of the mind's estrangement from sin,
when through long training in what is good we root sin out of ourselves completely, like some evil root, and this is innocence.
Or else innocence is lack of experience in wickedness, whether because of youth or because of some such way of life, when one is inexperienced in evil,
just as a little child knows neither arrogance nor guile nor trickery.
And again, there are some people living in villages who do not know the tricks of merchants and townspeople,
nor the twisting of words in the law courts, and we call such people innocent too,
not as having willingly separated themselves from vice and by their own struggle, but as not yet having experience of wickedness of mind.
But the truly innocent person is the one who is like David, who said:
"I walked in my blamelessness," who drove all vice from his soul through the struggle of the virtues, and who becomes worthy of the inheritance of good things.
For "the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk blamelessly." Such a person may say with hope:
"Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence," and again: "Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to my innocence that is in me."
But the straightforwardness and simplicity of his deeds portray the innocent man, such as Jacob was:
"an innocent man, dwelling in his own house," that is to say, he had a natural straightforwardness and displayed no artifice for people to see.

But in this place he calls "innocent" the one who is inexperienced in evil, who needs that praiseworthy shrewdness, so that on top of his natural straightforwardness he may also acquire knowledge through experience and,
as with a weapon, may be armed with that good shrewdness and not be brought down by his opponents.
For the perfect man must be wise toward what is good and innocent toward what is evil.
From this, as from a spring, the innocent receive that praiseworthy shrewdness.
"For a shrewd man is a seat of knowledge," and again he says:
"When evils came, the shrewd man hid himself." Now this word "shrewdness" means two things:
one is the man who is shrewd at harming his neighbour, which is wickedness; and the praiseworthy one is the shrewd [?]
the one who by sharpness and wisdom procures his own good and by cunning turns away from himself the things that come upon him from others.
Understand well, then, this word "shrewdness," and see that if someone uses it with a good mind for his own benefit,
he is praiseworthy, but the one who practices it to harm others is wicked and has it for his own destruction.
And the Scriptures are full of both these kinds.
For good was that stratagem of the Hebrews which they carried out against the Egyptians, when they both received from them the wages of their labor and acquired material for the tabernacle.
And again, those midwives used a good stratagem, for they preserved the Hebrew children;
good was that stratagem of Rebecca, who by deceit obtained that great blessing for her son;
Rahab and Rachel used a good stratagem, for the one saved the spies, while the other wisely delivered her father from idolatry.
But the Gibeonites devised an evil stratagem against the Israelites;
evil was that stratagem of Absalom, who under the appearance of kindness swayed many and rebelled against his father.
But here it signifies that good stratagem, which is like a weapon in this life and strengthens the souls of the ignorant.
If Eve had possessed this shrewdness, she would not have been deceived so easily.
For this teaching strengthens the innocent man, whose mind is easily led astray by believing every word, so that he may be knowledgeable and wise.
Let us see, then, further how it gives the young child knowledge and understanding.
For since man is twofold, as the Apostle says, the one outer and the other inner,
the one visible and the other invisible, it is evident that the ages of life too are to be understood in two ways.
For if someone should say that it would give bodily perception to a newborn child, that statement would be blameworthy, for what sense could the book give him,
since his eyes and ears and organs of smell and mouth and hands are born together with him, and this comes not by learning but by nature?
But it does not mean a bodily infant by "child," nor any one of these senses we have mentioned by "perception"; rather, this age must be understood as referring to the inner man.
For we have learned in many places in the Scriptures that there is both an infancy of the soul and an old age, as we have learned from the Apostle,
that the Corinthians were infants and for this reason still needed milk, which is the simple teaching of the Gospel, spoken to those who are new,
for they were not able to receive that perfect and solid food: the words of theology.
A youth in spirit, on the other hand, is one who has been perfected and strengthened in all the limbs of the virtues,
who is fervent in spirit, who is strong in the works of piety and courageous in everything good;
who is also called "violent" by the Gospel, for he is able to seize the kingdom of heaven; whom the Holy Spirit also takes up for singing praise, for it says:
"Young men and maidens, praise the name of the Lord," and again, it promises the young men in Israel that they will see visions.
And an old man in spirit is one who is perfect in wisdom, as Daniel was, and in the youth of his body the grey hairs of his wisdom were honorable.
For this reason those who were full of evil days said to him:
"Come and sit among us and speak to us, for God has given you old age."
So now here too it speaks of a little child, meaning one who has been born by that washing of the second birth, and has become like a child, and has thus been set on the way to the kingdom of heaven.
To such a newborn infant, then, who longs for that rational and guileless milk, this book of Proverbs gives knowledge and understanding:
knowledge of the affairs of this world, what they are like, and understanding of the age to come.
For it teaches him human matters as well and makes him knowledgeable in affairs, so that he may neither be a slave to evil desires,
nor be eager for this vain glory of the world; and then it also draws him to the understanding of that eternal age and by its words leads him to those good things that God has promised us.
Since, then, we have understood the distinctions of the ages with regard to the inner man, it is good
that we should also understand the names of the senses in the same way, as referring to the powers of the soul. And when he says:
"Incline your ear to my words," we must understand that he is seeking the soul's good hearing, as the Lord said:
"Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear," and by such words as these it gives that new child the sense of one who hears well.
And again, when it says, "Do not look at an evil woman," and, "Do not send your eyes toward her," and,
"Your eyes shall see rightly": it is evident that he grants sight to the spiritual child. And again, when he says:
"Eat honey, my son, that your palate may be sweetened," by honey he figuratively means the divine teaching, for it is said:
"Your words are sweeter to my palate than honey to my mouth." Through this teaching he brings spiritual tasting into the soul, about which it is said:
"Taste and see that the Lord is sweet." And again, the soul also has hands, by which wisdom touches it and draws it into sweet intimacy, for he says:
"Love her ardently, so that she may embrace you," and again in "Ecclesiastes" it says, "There is a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing."
For the body is defiled by the embrace of impurity, but the soul, by the embrace of wisdom, is wholly united with her and is filled with purity and beauty.
So he grants knowledge to the little child, and he gives understanding when he says:
"Possessions will not profit in the evil day." For by this saying he sows in your heart the remembrance of that day,
when an abundance of riches will not benefit you and will not be able to save you from the eternal fire. Or again, when he says:
"The blameless shall inherit the earth," in which the meek will also inherit, as the psalm cries out:
"The meek shall inherit the land," and again the Lord says, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land."
But when it says, "The wise shall inherit glory," it raises the soul to longing for the eternal good things.
This understanding it gives to the young child: fear of the torment of sinners and longing for the delight of the righteous, for "If a wise man hears these things, he will be wiser."
This saying of "Proverbs" testifies to great power, for it is higher than the wisdom of the wise,
and the words of this book surpass those other teachings of theirs, for the disciples of those other teachers are inexperienced, but those of this book are wise.
Since, then, many are called wise, for the resourceful of this world are also wise, and again those are wise
who have that true wisdom, our Lord Jesus Christ, within themselves through faith,
this it says about those who are outside that spiritual wisdom and know the wisdom of the world.
When they approach the teaching of "Proverbs," they become wiser, when they cast away that knowledge of vanity and all enter into the wonder of the truth.
And again, since "wise" is said in many ways, for one who is in longing for wisdom is called wise, and again,
one who has advanced in wisdom, and again, one who has been perfected in wisdom, whichever of these hears these words,
whether the lover of wisdom, or the one advancing in it, or the one perfected,
all will be wiser when they learn from this much teaching about divine matters and much about human ones.
For this book drives out wickedness in various ways and brings in virtue in many forms:
it bridles the lying tongue, restrains the eye that looks with evil, does not grant authority to unruly hands, banishes idleness, and chastises foul desires;
It teaches wisdom, it teaches justice, it teaches courage, it honors chastity.
And whoever learns all this and holds within himself flight from evil and the pursuit of good,
such a person, who was already wise because of his own desire, has become wiser through the perfection of this Scripture.
"But the prudent man shall acquire the art of steering," it says; for whoever intends to learn some art must possess by nature what that art requires:
that is, if someone is learning wrestling, he must have a good and strong build of body; and again, a swift runner must
be light and well-proportioned in his limbs; likewise a helmsman must have sharpness of mind and caution.
For this reason it does not call just any foolish man to the art of steering, but rather the prudent man. But what is this art of steering of which it speaks?
Surely it is nothing other than a certain art concerning the affairs of the soul and the unstable nature of human beings:
how could anyone be able to bring him across this world and this passing life,
which the Scriptures in many places call sea and river and water, as the Psalmist says:
"He sent from on high, he had mercy on me, and he took me up out of many waters."
For it is clear that he calls the turmoil of the world water, in which neither is its good firm and unshakable,
nor is its hardship unchanging, but all its affairs are in surging, tossing to and fro, and change.
For just as it is impossible for the sea to stay in one state for a long time, but what is now calm is after a little while stirred up by waves;
and again, what is stirred up and boiling with waves, a great stillness calms once more; so too the affairs of this world easily change into one thing and another.
For this reason a helmsman is needed, so that even in the time of calm, when everything is in abundance for him,
he may expect that change and not rejoice over passing things as if they were immortal.
And again, in the time of affliction he should not cut off his hope, nor be drowned by immoderate grief.
For neither the health of the body, nor the flower of youth, nor the prosperity of the household, nor the other good things of this age last for a long time,
but when you are in the fair weather of this life, expect at some point also the winter of affairs,
for sickness will come and poverty will come, since the breeze of the wind does not always stand behind you, but also from the front,
it often blows head-on; and whoever is fearless and glorious, unexpected trials reach him like fierce winds and shake him.
And the successive onsets of afflictions are like waves, and they come one upon another and throw you into turmoil.
But the time will come again, and you will see them all passed away and the same calm returned.
This, then, is the prudent helmsman: one who knows the weakness and instability of this life, and is always the same, and does not boast in the time of ease,
nor in the time of trial be despairing and distressed. And again, for another matter too, that use of the pilot's art is good for us,
for I know other waves as well, and a sea terribly stirred up against the soul, which are the evil passions.
For angers and fears, desires and griefs: these come on like evil waves, and often, when they find a soul without a pilot, they sink it.
Now therefore the mind must, like a pilot, sit above all the passions and be mounted on its own flesh as on a ship, and with the skill of its thoughts,
as with rudders, it must steer and bravely trample down those passions, those evil waves, and not be filled with their bitterness, but pray and say:
"Let me be delivered from those who hate me and from the depths of many waters. Let not the whirlpool of waters drown me, nor the depth of the abyss cover me."
Do you wish me to show you another kind of piloting too, whose gift is good?
"The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant man," and all of us who walk this road of the Gospel are merchants, who buy the kingdom of heaven by fulfilling the commandments.
It is right for us, then, to acquire and gather great and manifold wealth of the kingdom of heaven, so that we may not be put to shame at that time
when each one shows his deeds, like those servants who received the talent from the Lord, so that we may not hear:
"Evil and slothful servant," but rather so that we may fill our ship with good cargo and thus pass through this life without going astray.
For many have gathered much from their youth, and just when they reached the middle of the road, or had come near the end,
trials of waves rose against them from the evil spirits, and they could not endure the severity of that storm,
for they did not know the pilot's art, and great distress came upon them from all this.
For this reason some were sunk with regard to the faith and became wrong believers, and others in turn
lost the virginity they had kept from childhood, because that evil desire came upon them like a fierce gale and destroyed them.
And then the matter is pitiable: a man, after fasting and severe ascetic struggle, after mighty prayer,
after much weeping and a contest of twenty or thirty years, through negligence of soul is stripped of all this in an instant, and he resembles a great and rich merchant

who has filled his ship with great wealth and sails with a pleasant wind from behind, and has passed through those terrible seas, and just as he nears the harbor the ship is shattered and in an instant he is bereft of it all.
So it is also with the soul, if it too, by a single attack of the devil, loses all those good things acquired with much labor and sweat, and,
As in some raging mist, so he is drowned in sins, and then the saying will fit him well:
"I came into the depth of the sea, and the tempest drowned me."
Therefore keep the rudders of life well in hand and direct your eyes, lest through the eyes that evil wave of desire burst in upon you;
Steer your hearing and your tongue, lest your hearing take in something harmful, lest you say something improper.
Lest the surge of anger stir you up, lest the current of wicked fear swallow you, lest the whirlpool of wrath cover you over.
For the passions are waves, and if you rise above them, then you are a wise helmsman.
But if you do not flee from all these things with haste, but are tossed about on every side by the waves like a ship with no crew, you will vanish in the abyss of sin.
Hear, then, this also, how you may learn the art of helmsmanship: for sailors are accustomed to look to the sky and in this way to know
how the ship ought to be steered: by day from the sun, and by night from the Hyades [?], or the Pleiades [?], or the other bright stars.
Likewise, then, may you too keep your eyes on heaven, in keeping with the word of the speaker who said:
"To you, Lord, who dwell in the heavens, I lifted up my eyes."
Look to the Sun of Righteousness and to the commandments of the Lord, as to bright stars.
Keep a watchful eye; give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, for if you never doze while holding the rudder on this sea of the world,
then you will also find the help of the Holy Spirit to guide you with a calm and pleasant breeze, until you reach the waveless harbor of life and of the will of God,
to whom belong glory and might through the endless ages, forever and ever, amen.
